      <title>Meshery Community</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/community/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/community/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery is a CNCF project maintained by engineers from VMware, Red Hat, Rackspace, Citrix, Instabase, Microsoft, OpenGov, Computas AS, Rill Data, Quantex, Lumina Networks, API7, F5, Citi, Acquia, and HashiCorp. Meshery is an open source project that adheres to the <a href="https://github.com/cncf/foundation/blob/master/code-of-conduct.md">CNCF&rsquo;s Code of Conduct</a>. Meshery advance the state of the art surrounding cloud native management and enable adopters of Cloud Native technologies and techniques to do so with confidence. Our shared commitment to the open source spirit pushes Meshery forward.</p></description>
    </item>

    <item>
      <title>Cloud Native Design Patterns</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/pattern-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/pattern-management/</guid>
      <description><div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">What are Cloud Native Patterns?</div>
<p>This feature area is under active development. Patterns will be importable and exportable as OCI images in v0.8.0.</p>
</div>
<p>Patterns are essentially atomic designs with one or more components made in composed into an atomic, reusable design. Patterns are a way to apply the DRY principle when managing the configuration of cloud native infrastructure.</p>
<h2 id="use-meshery-to-deploy-a-cloud-native-pattern">
	Use Meshery to Deploy a Cloud Native Pattern
</h2>
<p>Use Meshery to deploy a cloud native pattern. Cloud native patterns are detailed as a YAML file. See the <a href="/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/">Configuration Management</a> guide.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Configuration Management Guides</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/</guid>
      <description><p>Guides for understanding Meshery&rsquo;s ability to configure infrastructure and applications.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Configuring your Cloud Native Infrastructure and Applications</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/working-with-designs/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/working-with-designs/</guid>
      <description><p>As an cloud native management platform, Meshery has built-in support infastructure and application configuration management. Use Meshery to configure your multi-cluster Kubernetes environments on-premises or across clouds.</p>
<h2 id="what-is-a-meshery-design">
	What is a Meshery Design?
</h2>
<p>Meshery&rsquo;s core construct of configuration management is that of a design. A design is ultimately a document – and a document in which you capture and describe your desired state of improv the environment.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/working-with-designs/images/context-aware-design.svg"><img class="content-image" src="./images/context-aware-design.svg" alt="Context Aware Design"  /></a></p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Create Models</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/creating-models/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/creating-models/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery offers two primary ways to bring models into your system: <strong>Create</strong> and <strong><a href="/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/importing-models/">Import</a></strong>.</p>
<ul>
<li><strong>Import</strong> is ideal when you already have a model definition file (e.g., JSON, CSV) and simply want to bring it into Meshery.</li>
<li><strong>Create</strong> is the recommended approach if you’re starting fresh — it guides you through building a model step by step using an intuitive UI wizard.</li>
</ul>
<p>This section walks you through the <strong>Create</strong> workflow — perfect for users who want full control over naming, styling, and categorizing their models while sourcing CRDs from GitHub or ArtifactHub.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Creating a Meshery Design</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/creating-a-meshery-design/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/creating-a-meshery-design/</guid>
      <description><div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Learn about Designs</div>
<p>Learn more about <a href='/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs'>what a Meshery Design</a> is and how it fits into Meshery&rsquo;s approach to cloud native management.</p>
</div>
<h2 id="ways-to-create-a-meshery-design">
	Ways to create a Meshery Design
</h2>
<p>You can create a Meshery design in two ways:</p>
<h3 id="from-scratch">
	From scratch
</h3>
<ol>
<li>Click on the &ldquo;Design&rdquo; tab to start creating a new design.</li>
<li>In the left panel, click &ldquo;Components&rdquo; and browse the type of component you want to add.</li>
<li>Drag and drop the components onto the canvas.</li>
<li>Click and drag from one component to another to create connections between components. You can customize the connections by adding labels or adjusting their properties.</li>
<li>Once you&rsquo;re satisfied with your design, click the &ldquo;Save&rdquo; button on the toolbar. Your design will be saved as &ldquo;Untitled design&rdquo; by default. You can give your design a name to help identify and manage it later.</li>
</ol>
<h3 id="from-a-template">
	From a template
</h3>
<p>Another way to create a Meshery design is to use an already curated template. You can either import designs that others have published and made available for public use or clone patterns from the Meshery Catalog.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Edge Styles Guide</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/edges-guide/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/edges-guide/</guid>
      <description><p>In Meshery, the line that connects <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">components</a> is called an <strong>edge</strong>. Each edge visually represents a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/">relationship</a> and uses a specific style to communicate its nature.</p>
<p>This guide helps you interpret the most common edge styles you will encounter.</p>
<h3 id="interpreting-common-edge-styles">
	Interpreting Common Edge Styles
</h3>
<p>Meshery uses a set of default visual styles to provide at-a-glance information about the type of connection an edge represents. While these styles can be customized in the UI, understanding the defaults is key to interpreting component relationships.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Exporting Models</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/exporting-models/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/exporting-models/</guid>
      <description><p>Export existing Meshery <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Models</a> or your custom infrastructure crd imported as <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Models</a> in Meshery. The platform supports a variety of application definition formats, and you can export designs using either the Meshery CLI or the Meshery UI.</p>
<h2 id="export-models-using-meshery-cli">
	Export Models Using Meshery CLI
</h2>
<p><strong>Step 1: Install Meshery CLI</strong></p>
<p>Before you can use the Meshery CLI to export a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Model</a>, you must first install it. You can install Meshery CLI by <a href="/v0.9/installation/#install-mesheryctl">following the instructions</a>.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Identifying Meshery Components</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/identifying-components/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/identifying-components/</guid>
      <description><p>Ever wondered what the different icons and shapes in Meshery represent? Whether you&rsquo;re looking at a dashboard, a settings page, or a design, you&rsquo;ll encounter a rich library of visual elements. This guide is here to help you understand what they mean.</p>
<p>The <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">components</a> in Meshery fall into two fundamental categories, distinguished by whether they can be orchestrated (managed) by Meshery during deployment:</p>
<ul>
<li>
<p><strong>Semantic Components (Orchestratable):</strong> These represent actual infrastructure resources that Meshery can understand and manage during deployment. Examples include Kubernetes resources (like Pods and Services), databases, and other infrastructure components. Meshery will actively manage their lifecycle during deployment.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Importing Models</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/importing-models/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/importing-models/</guid>
      <description><p>Import your existing Models and existing custom resource definition (CRD) into Meshery. The platform supports a variety of application definition formats, and you can import designs using either the Meshery CLI or the Meshery UI.</p>
<p><strong>Note:</strong> A <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Model</a> can be only imported if it contains atleast a valid <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Component</a> or <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/relationships/">Relationship</a>.</p>
<h2 id="import-models-using-meshery-cli">
	Import Models Using Meshery CLI
</h2>
<div class="alert alert-warning" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Limitation on Importing Connections</div>
<p>The <code>mesheryctl model import</code> command currently supports importing Models containing Components, Relationships, and Policies. Importing Models with <code>Connection</code> definitions is not yet supported. This functionality may be added in a future release.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Push or Pull a Model Image</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/push-pull-model-image/</lin

k>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/configuration-management/push-pull-model-image/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="use-mesheryctl-to-push-or-pull-a-model-image">
	Use mesheryctl to Push or Pull a Model Image
</h2>
<p>You can push or pull Meshery model images to or from any OCI-compatible image repository.</p></description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

    <item>
      <title>Build & Release (CI)</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/build-and-release/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/build-and-release/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery’s build and release system incorporates many tools, organized into different workflows each triggered by different events. Meshery’s build and release system does not run on a schedule, but is event-driven. GitHub Actions are used to define Meshery’s CI workflows. New builds of Meshery and its various components are automatically generated upon push, release, and other similar events, typically in relation to their respective master branches.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Meshery Test Documents</div>
<p>The Meshery Test Strategy (<a href='https://docs.google.com/document/d/11nAxYtz2SUusCYZ0JeNRrOLIxkgmmbUVWz63MBZV2oE/edit'>1</a>,<a href='https://docs.google.com/document/d/14vbwnKafqxrr-cJOmLWEvvj75MFrxFKiUdfPwZRhg64/edit'>2</a>) is a comprehensive document that outlines the approach to testing, types of tests, frameworks used - test strategy - for each of Meshery&rsquo;s architectural components. The <a href='https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/13Ir4gfaKoAX9r8qYjAFFl_U9ntke4X5ndREY1T7bnVs/edit'>Meshery Test Plan</a> is a tactical spreadsheet that <em>itemizes</em> specific integration and end-to-end test cases and tracks their status. It includes a list of GitHub workflows and their purpose. Join the <a href='https://docs.google.com/document/d/1GrVdGHZAYeu6wHNLLoiaKNqBtk7enXE9XeDRCvdA4bY/edit#'>Meshery CI meeting</a> and/or the <a href='https://meshery.io/subscribe'>developers mailing list</a> to get involved. </div></p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Contributing</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/</guid>
      <description><h1 id="contributing">
	Contributing
</h1>
<p>Please do! Thanks for your help! 🎈 Meshery is community-built and welcomes collaboration. Contributors are expected to adhere to the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/blob/master/CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md">CNCF&rsquo;s Code of Conduct</a>.</p>
<h2 id="general-contribution-flow">
	General Contribution Flow
</h2>
<p>Meshery and it&rsquo;s various architectural components are written in different languages, including Golang, Javascript (React.js and Next.js) To make building, testing, and the experience of contributing consistent across all Meshery components, a <code>Makefile</code> is included in the every repository. These <code>make</code> targets are what you will use to build, run, test, and document.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Contributing to Meshery Adapters</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-adapters/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-adapters/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery Adapters are the Extension Points in Meshery&rsquo;s architecture. Their design, the process of creating a new adapter is documented in <a href="/v0.9/extensibility/adapters">Extensibility: Meshery Adapters</a>.</p>
<p>With the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/blob/master/CONTRIBUTING.md#adapter">CONTRIBUTING.md</a> in mind, understand that development follows the usual fork-and-pull request workflow described here, see also GitHub Process. On forking GitHub deactivates all workflows. It is safe and good practice to activate them such that the code is validated on each push. This requires that branches filter for “on push” is set to ‘**’ to be triggered also on branches containing ‘/’  in their name.  The actions are parameterized using secrets (see Build &amp; Release Strategy). The Docker image is only built and pushed to Docker Hub if a tag is pushed and the corresponding authentication information is configured.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Contributing to Meshery CLI</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli/</guid>
      <description><p><code>mesheryctl</code> is written in Golang or the Go Programming Language. For development use <a href="https://go.dev/dl/">Go version 1.25+</a>. <code>mesheryctl</code> uses the <a href="https://github.com/spf13/cobra">Cobra</a> framework. A good first-step towards contributing to <code>mesheryctl</code> would be to familiarize yourself with the <a href="https://github.com/spf13/cobra#concepts">Cobra concepts</a>. For manipulating config files, <code>mesheryctl</code> uses <a href="https://github.com/spf13/viper">Viper</a>.</p>
<div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">Meshery CLI Reference Documents</div>
<ul><li><a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1q63sIGAuCnIeDs8PeM-0BAkNj8BBgPUXhLbe1Y-318o/edit#gid=0">Meshery Command Tracker</a>: Status of mesheryctl command implementation and platform compatibility.</li>
    <li><a href="https://docs.google.com/document/d/1xRlFpElRmybJ3WacgPKXgCSiQ2poJl3iCCV1dAalf0k/edit#">Meshery CLI Commands and Documentation</a>: Detailed documentation of the `mesheryctl` commands.</li>
    <li><a href="https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/13Ir4gfaKoAX9r8qYjAFFl_U9ntke4X5ndREY1T7bnVs/edit?gid=1907616946#gid=1907616946">Meshery Test Plan</a>: Test cases for end-to-end testing of Meshery functionality.</li>
	<li><a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/labels/component%2Fmesheryctl">mesheryctl open issues and pull requests</a>: Matching the "component/mesheryctl" label.</li></ul></div>
<h3 id="designing-commands">
	Designing Commands
</h3>
<p>The <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli-guide/">Meshery CLI Style Guide</a> outlines the process by which new commands are designed and contains a collection of principles and conventions that need to be followed while designing <code>mesheryctl</code> commands. <code>mesheryctl</code> might be the interface that the users first have with Meshery. As such, <code>mesheryctl</code> needs to provide a great UX.</p></description>
    </item>

      <description><p>Meshery CLI is the command line interface for Meshery.     <item>
      <title>Contributing to Meshery Policies</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project

/contributing/contributing-policies/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-policies/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="background">
	Background
</h2>
<p>Meshery has a built-in policy engine, based on <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/">Open Policy Agent (OPA)</a>. Meshery uses the <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/policy-language/">Rego</a> query language to create these <a href="https://docs.meshery.io/concepts/logical/policies">policies</a>.</p>
<h2 id="prerequisites">
	Prerequisites
</h2>
<p>To start contributing to Meshery Policy Engine, make sure you have <a href="https://www.openpolicyagent.org/docs/latest/#running-opa">OPA CLI</a> installed on your system. You will also need to clone the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/">Meshery Server</a> project from Github.</p>
<h2 id="components-of-meshery-policy-engine">
	Components of Meshery Policy Engine
</h2>
<p>Rego policies are the declarative logic behind the policy engine. These policies define how the underlying engine understands relationships within Meshery Designs. Rego policies can be found <a href="https://github.com/meshery/meshery/tree/master/server/meshmodel/meshery-core/0.7.2/v1.0.0/policies">here</a> in the Meshery Github repository.</p></description>
    </item>

Use <code>make</code> to build any and all components.</p>

</h2>

    <item>
      <title>Contributing to Model Components</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-components/</guid>
      <description><p><strong>Components are defined by schemas.</strong> Each component&rsquo;s structure, capabilities, and metadata follow the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1beta1/component">Component schema</a> in <code>meshery/schemas</code>. When creating or modifying components, ensure they conform to the schema specification. See <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-schemas/">Contributing to Schemas</a> for details.</p>
<p>In Meshery, a <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Components</a> is a fundamental building block used to represent and define the infrastructure under management. Each component provides granular and specific support for your infrastructure and applications. Once registered with Meshery Server (in the <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/registry/">Registry</a>), components are available for inclusion in <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a> that you create. Components can be created and published by anyone, allowing you to share you custom extensions with the community.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Contributing to Model Relationships</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-relationships/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>

      <description><p><strong>Relationships follow a schema-defined structure.</strong> The <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1alpha3/relationship">Relationship schema</a> specifies how relationships between components are expressed.       <description><p><strong>Meshery Models are schema-driven.</strong> Model definitions, including their structure, metadata, and versioning, are defined by JSON Schemas in the <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas"><code>meshery/schemas</code></a> repository. </h2>
<p>Meshery uses a logical object model to describe the infrastructure and capabilities it manages in a consistent and extensible way.</p>
<h4 id="what-are-meshery-models">

      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-models-quick-start/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-models-quick-start/</guid>
      <description><p><strong>Models follow Meshery&rsquo;s schema-driven development approach.</strong> Model, Component, and Relationship definitions are validated against schemas in <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/tree/master/schemas/constructs/v1beta1/model"><code>Model schema</code></a>. See <a href="/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-schemas/">Contributing to Schemas</a> for details.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/models/">Meshery Models</a> are a way to represent the architecture of a system or application. Models are defined in JSON and can be used to visualize the components and relationships between them. This guide will walk you through the process of creating a new model.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/components/">Meshery Components</a> are the building blocks of a model. Each component represents a different part of the system or application. Components can be anything from a database to a microservice to a server. Relationships define how components interact with each other. For example, a database component might have a relationship with a microservice component that represents the microservice&rsquo;s dependency on the database.</p></description>

      <description><p>Meshery pervasively uses MeshKit as a golang and infrastructure management-specific library in all of its components. MeshKit helps populate error messages with a uniform and useful set of informative attributes.</p>

It extracts error details into a file that can be used for publishing all error code references on the Meshery <a href="/v0.9/reference/error-codes/">error codes reference page</a>. The objective to create this was to avoid centralized handling of error codes and automating everything</p></description>

    <item>
      <title>Meshery CLI Style Guide</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli-guide/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/contributing/contributing-cli-guide/</guid>
      <description><p>These guidelines are a collection of principles and conventions that need to be followed while designing mesheryctl commands.</p>
<h2 id="design-principles">
	Design Principles
</h2>
<p><strong>1. Consistency is quality.</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><em>Consistency of interaction drives a quality user experience. Whether that experience is delightful or painful is a related, but separate consideration. Meshery&rsquo;s behavior of user interactions should be consistent even when their user experience is poor.</em></li>
</ul>
<p>Consistency is key when designing intuitive interfaces. Although <code>mesheryctl perf run -f &lt;performance profile name&gt;</code> may sound more intuitive, users who are experienced in using the CLI will prefer the consistent verb <code>apply</code> over <code>run</code>. This will also ensure a consistent command language making memorizing easier. Consistency should also be enforced when chaining commands and using flags.</p></description>
    </item>

<ul>

<li><strong>Advanced Users</strong>: Those who already have some experience and want deeper insights or specialized use cases.</li>
</ul>
</li>
<li>
<p><strong>Contributors &amp; System Integrators</strong></p></description>

      <description><div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">MeshSync</div>
<p>Managed by the <a href='/v0.9/concepts/architecture/operator'>Meshery Operator</a>, MeshSync is a custom Kubernetes controller that provides tiered discovery and continual synchronization with Meshery Server as to the state of the Kubernetes clusters and their workloads. Learn more about <a href='/v0.9/concepts/architecture/meshsync'>MeshSync</a>.</p>
</div>
<p>MeshSync is your tool for efficient management and synchronization of Kubernetes clusters! This user guide will walk you through how to establish a connection with any element that Meshery is able to connect to and manage. Use the MeshSync page to register connections, view connection metadata, and perform connectivity tests, as weel as to manage credentials and environments.</p></description>

      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/overview/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="using-meshery-designs-to-manage-your-infrastructure">
	Using Meshery Designs to Manage Your Infrastructure
</h2>
<p>Meshery is a versatile platform designed to streamline the lifecycle, configuration, and performance management of infrastructure across Kubernetes clusters.</p>
<h3 id="designs-in-meshery">
	Designs in Meshery
</h3>
<p>Meshery employs the concept of <a href="/v0.9/concepts/logical/designs/">Designs</a> as a fundamental construct for managing infrastructure. Designs provide a structured way to organize and deploy various components of your infrastructure. To do so, Meshery utilizes a declarative approach to infrastructure management, similar to Kubernetes manifests. Meshery Designs are written in YAML and are validated against a schema.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Infrastructure Management Guides</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/</guid>
      <description><p>Guides for understanding Meshery&rsquo;s ability to manage infrastructure.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Managing Connections</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/lifecycle-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/lifecycle-management/</guid>
      <description><p><a name="lifecycle-management"></a></p>
<p>Meshery manages hundreds of different types of cloud native infrastructure. See the <a href="/v0.9/extensibility/integrations">full set of integrations</a>.</p>
<h2 id="cloud-native-infrastructure-lifecycle-management">
	Cloud Native Infrastructure Lifecycle Management
</h2>
<p><a href="/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/lifecycle-management/images/states-for-kubernetes-cluster-connections.svg"><img class="content-image" src="./images/states-for-kubernetes-cluster-connections.svg" alt="Lifecycle Management"  /></a></p>
<p>Meshery Adapters can optionally be deployed to provide deep support of different types of infrastructure, so that you can learn and compare different infrastructure functionality. Once you have selected to operate a given infrastructure, Meshery will assist you with ongoing operations.</p>
<p>Meshery automates the provisioning of various infrastructurees, allowing users to select different configuration profiles in order to support a variety of deployment models.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Managing Events with Notification Center</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/notification-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/infrastructure-management/notification-management/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery continuously tracks activities affecting your infrastructure and workloads. Meshery generates a variety of events, reflecting activities affecting the design and operation of your infrastructure whether those activities are directly or indirectly performed through Meshery operations.</p>
<h3 id="what-is-the-notification-center">
	What is the Notification Center?
</h3>
<p>The Notification Center is a dedicated panel in Meshery’s UI that helps you monitor, understand, and respond to events across your system. It acts as a central place where you can see important updates related to your infrastructure, workloads, and Meshery’s internal operations.</p></description>
    </item>
  </channel>

      <title>Upgrading Meshery and all of its components</title>
      <link>/v0.9/installation/upgrades/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/installation/upgrades/</guid>
      <description><h1 id="upgrade-guide">
	Upgrade Guide
</h1>
<h2 id="upgrading-meshery-server-adapters-and-ui">
	Upgrading Meshery Server, Adapters, and UI
</h2>
<p>Various components of Meshery will need to be upgraded as new releases become available. Meshery is comprised of a number of components including a server, adapters, UI, and CLI. As an application, Meshery is a composition of different functional components.</p>
<p style="text-align:center">
<a href="./images/upgrading-meshery.svg">
    <img src="./images/upgrading-meshery.svg" style="margin: 1rem;" />
</a><br /><i><small>Figure: Meshery components</small></i>
</p>
<p>Some of the components must be upgraded simultaneously, while others may be upgraded independently. The following table depicts components, their versions, and deployment units (deployment groups).</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Using Multiple Adapters</title>
      <link>/v0.9/installation/multiple-adapters/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/installation/multiple-adapters/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="advanced-configuration">
	Advanced Configuration
</h2>
<p>Meshery is capable of running zero or more adapters. Meshery offers many features without the need for adapters. Adapters are optional components that enhance and extend Meshery&rsquo;s core functionality.</p>
<h3 id="modifying-the-default-adapter-deployment-configuration">
	Modifying the default adapter deployment configuration
</h3>
<p>The number of adapters, type of adapters, where they are deployed, how they are named and what port they are exposed on are all configurable deployment options. To modify the default configuration, find <code>~/.meshery/meshery.yaml</code> on your system. <code>~/.meshery/meshery.yaml</code> is a Docker Compose file.</p></description>
    </item>
  </channel>

      <description><h1>Quick Start with AKS <img src="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/images/aks.svg" style="width:35px;height:35px;" /></h1>
<p>Manage your AKS clusters with Meshery. Deploy Meshery in AKS <a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#in-cluster-installation">in-cluster</a> or outside of AKS <a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#out-of-cluster-installation">out-of-cluster</a>. <strong><em>Note: It is advisable to install Meshery in your AKS clusters</em></strong></p>
<div class="prereqs"><h4>Prerequisites</h4>
<ol>
<li>Install the Meshery command line client, <a href="/v0.9/installation/mesheryctl" class="meshery-light">mesheryctl</a>.</li>
<li>Install <a href="https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/tools/">kubectl</a> on your local machine.</li>
<li>Install <a href="https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cli/azure/install-azure-cli">Azure CLI</a>, configured for your environment.</li>
<li>Access to an active AKS cluster in one of your resource groups.</li>
</ol>
</div>
<p>Also see: <a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/">Install Meshery on Kubernetes</a></p>
<h2 id="available-deployment-methods">
	Available Deployment Methods
</h2>
<ul>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#in-cluster-installation">In-cluster Installation</a>
<ul>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#preflight-checks">Preflight Checks</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#preflight-cluster-connectivity">Preflight: Cluster Connectivity</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#installation-using-mesheryctl">Installation: Using <code>mesheryctl</code></a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#installation-using-helm">Installation: Using Helm</a></li>
<li><a href="/v0.9/installation/kubernetes/aks/#post-installation-steps">Post-Installation Steps</a></li>
</ul>
</li>
</ul>
<h1 id="in-cluster-installation">
	In-cluster Installation
</h1>
<p>Follow the steps below to install Meshery in your AKS cluster.</p></description>

      <description><h1 id="install-meshery-on-kubernetes-using-helm">
	Install Meshery on Kubernetes Using Helm
</h1>
<div class="prereqs"><h4>Prerequisites</h4>
<ol>
<li><a href="https://helm.sh/docs/intro/install/" class="meshery-light">Helm</a> should be installed on your local machine.</li>
<li>You should have access to the cluster/platform where you want to deploy Meshery.</li>
<li>Ensure that the kubeconfig file has the correct current context/cluster configuration.</li>
</ol>
</div>
<h2 id="install-meshery-on-your-kubernetes-cluster-using-helm">
	Install Meshery on Your Kubernetes Cluster Using Helm
</h2>


<pre class="codeblock-pre">
	<div class="codeblock">
		<code class="clipboardjs">helm repo add meshery https://meshery.io/charts/
helm install meshery meshery/meshery --namespace meshery --create-namespace</code>
	</div>
</pre>

<p>Optionally, Meshery Server supports customizing the callback URL for your remote provider, like so:</p></description>

      <title>Authenticating Meshery via CLI</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/authenticate-with-meshery-via-cli/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/authenticate-with-meshery-via-cli/</guid>
      <description><p>To authenticate Meshery through <code>mesheryctl</code>, the Meshery CLI, you will use the <code>mesheryctl system login</code> command. On executing this command, you will be provided with a list of providers to choose from. You can then select a Provider of your choice to complete the authentication and authorization process.</p>
<p>As of this writing, you will be presented with two providers, <em>Meshery</em> and <em>None</em>.</p>
<div class="highlight"><pre tabindex="0" class="chroma"><code class="language-bash" data-lang="bash"><span class="line"><span class="cl">Use the arrow keys to navigate: ↓ ↑ → ← 
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">? Select a Provider: 
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">  ▸ Meshery
</span></span><span class="line"><span class="cl">    None
</span></span></code></pre></div><ul>
<li>
<p>Selecting <em>Meshery</em> will open a browser to complete the login and authentication process with Meshery Cloud. On successful authentication, you can close the window and return to the command prompt.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Bash</title>
      <link>/v0.9/installation/linux-mac/bash/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/installation/linux-mac/bash/</guid>
      <description><h1 id="install-meshery-cli-with-bash">
	Install Meshery CLI with Bash
</h1>
<p>To install or upgrade <code>mesheryctl</code> using <code>bash</code>, execute anyone of the following commands.</p>
<h4 id="option-1-only-install-mesheryctl-binary">
	Option 1: Only install <code>mesheryctl</code> binary
</h4>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre">
 <div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">
  $ curl -L https://meshery.io/install | DEPLOY_MESHERY=false bash -
 </div></div>
 </pre>
<br />
<br />
#### Option 2: Install `mesheryctl` binary and deploy Meshery on Docker
 <pre class="codeblock-pre">
 <div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">
  $ curl -L https://meshery.io/install | PLATFORM=docker bash -
 </div></div>
 </pre>
<br />
<br />
#### Option 3: Install `mesheryctl` binary and deploy Meshery on Kubernetes
 <pre class="codeblock-pre">
 <div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">
  $ curl -L https://meshery.io/install | PLATFORM=kubernetes bash -
 </div></div>
 </pre>
<br />
<br />
#### Option 4: Install `mesheryctl` binary and Meshery adapter(s)
<p>Install <code>mesheryctl</code> binary and include one or more <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/adapters/">adapters</a> to be deployed</p></description>
    </item>

      <description><h1 id="install-meshery-cli-with-homebrew">

<p>You need to have <code>Brew</code> installed on your <strong>Linux</strong> or <strong>macOS</strong> system to perform these actions.</p>

<p>To install <code>mesheryctl</code> using homebrew, execute the following commands.</p>

      <title>Configuring Autocompletion for `mesheryctl`</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/configuring-autocompletion-for-mesheryctl/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/configuring-autocompletion-for-mesheryctl/</guid>
      <description><p>If you would like to have <code>mesheryctl</code> commands automatically completed for use as you use <code>mesheryctl</code>, then use the following instructions to configure automatic completion within your environment.</p>
<h2 id="autocompletion-for-bash">
	Autocompletion for Bash
</h2>
<h3 id="bash--32">
	bash &lt;= 3.2
</h3>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">source /dev/stdin <<< "$(mesheryctl completion bash)"</div></div>
 </pre>
<h3 id="bash--40">
	bash &gt;= 4.0
</h3>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">source <(mesheryctl completion bash)</div></div>
 </pre>
<h3 id="bash--32-on-macos">
	bash &lt;= 3.2 on MacOS
</h3>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">brew install bash-completion # ensure you have bash-completion 1.3+
mesheryctl completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/mesheryctl</div></div>
 </pre>
<h3 id="bash--40-on-macos">
	bash &gt;= 4.0 on MacOS
</h3>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">brew install bash-completion@2
mesheryctl completion bash > $(brew --prefix)/etc/bash_completion.d/mesheryctl</div></div>
 </pre>
<h2 id="autocompletion-for-zsh">
	Autocompletion for zsh
</h2>
 <pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
 <div class="clipboardjs">source <(mesheryctl completion zsh)</div></div>
 </pre><br>
<p>If shell completion is not already enabled in your environment you will need to enable it. You can execute the following once:</p></description>
    </item>

      <title>Mesheryctl system commands</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/system-commands/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/system-commands/</guid>
      <description><p>Let&rsquo;s get familiar with mesheryctl system commands. The syntax of the mesheryctl commands goes as follws : <code>mesheryctl &lt;Main_command&gt; &lt;Argument&gt; &lt;Flags&gt;</code></p>
<h2 id="main_command--system">
	Main_command : system
</h2>
<h3 id="start">
	start
</h3>
<p><code>mesheryctl system start</code> : This will initiate Meshery &amp; automatically open it in your default web browser.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/images/start.png"><img alt="skip-browser" style="width:500px;height:auto;" src="/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/images/start.png" /></a></p>
<p><code>mesheryctl system start --skip-browser</code> : It skips opening Meshery in your browser with the provided URL.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/images/skipbrowser.png"><img alt="skip-browser" style="width:500px;height:auto;" src="/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/images/skipbrowser.png" /></a></p>
<p><code>mesheryctl system start --skip-update</code> : It is used when you want to skip updating Meshery if an update is available.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Running system checks using Meshery CLI</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/running-system-checks-using-mesheryctl/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/running-system-checks-using-mesheryctl/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery&rsquo;s CLI, <code>mesheryctl</code>, includes commands for verifying system readiness for a Meshery deployment and health checks to confirm the health of an existing Meshery deployment. Whether you have yet to deploy Meshery or have already deployed Meshery, <code>mesheryctl system check</code> is a useful utility to ensure that your Meshery deployments are healthy.</p>
<pre class="codeblock-pre">
<div class="codeblock"><div class="clipboardjs">mesheryctl system check</div></div>
</pre>
<p><br/><p>
<pre class="codeblock-pre">
<div class="codeblock"><div class="clipboardjs">Verify environment pre/post-deployment of Meshery.
<p>Usage:
mesheryctl system check [flags]</p>
<p>Flags:
&ndash;adapter Check status of Meshery adapters
-h, &ndash;help help for check
&ndash;operator Check status of Meshery operators
&ndash;pre Verify environment readiness to deploy Meshery
&ndash;preflight Verify environment readiness to deploy Meshery</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Scoop</title>
      <link>/v0.9/installation/windows/scoop/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/installation/windows/scoop/</guid>
      <description><h1 id="install-meshery-cli-with-scoop">
	Install Meshery CLI with Scoop
</h1>
<h2 id="prerequisites">
	Prerequisites
</h2>
<p>You need to have <code>scoop</code> installed on your Windows system to perform these actions.</p>
<h3 id="install-mesheryctl-with-scoop">
	Install <code>mesheryctl</code> with Scoop
</h3>
<p>To install <code>mesheryctl</code> using Scoop, execute the following commands.</p>
<pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
<div class="clipboardjs">scoop bucket add mesheryctl https://github.com/meshery/scoop-bucket.git
scoop install mesheryctl</div></div>
</pre>
<p>You&rsquo;re ready to run Meshery. To do so, execute the following command.</p>
<pre class="codeblock-pre"><div class="codeblock">
<div class="clipboardjs">mesheryctl system start</div></div>
</pre>
<p>If you are running Meshery on Docker, execute the following command.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Using Meshery CLI</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/working-with-mesheryctl/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/mesheryctl/working-with-mesheryctl/</guid>
      <description><p>Meshery&rsquo;s command line interface is <code>mesheryctl</code>. Use <code>mesheryctl</code> to both manage the lifecyle of Meshery itself and to access and invoke any of Meshery&rsquo;s application and cloud native management functions. <code>mesheryctl</code> commands can be categorized as follows:</p>
<ul>
<li><code>mesheryctl</code> - Global overrides and flags</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl app</code> - Cloud Native Application Management</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl filter</code> - Cloud Native Filter Management</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl mesh</code> - Cloud Native Lifecycle &amp; Configuration Management</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl perf</code> - Cloud Native Performance Management</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl design</code> - Cloud Native Pattern Configuration &amp; Management</li>
<li><code>mesheryctl system</code> - Meshery Lifecycle and Troubleshooting</li>
</ul>
<h2 id="configuring-meshery-deployments-with-meshconfig">
	Configuring Meshery Deployments with meshconfig
</h2>
<p><em>Meshconfig</em> refers to a configuration file found at <code>~/.meshery/config.yaml</code>. Your meshconfig file must contain one or more <code>contexts</code> in order for any <code>mesheryctl system</code> command to work. Each context represents a Meshery deployment.</p></description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

      <title>Interpreting Performance Test Results</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/interpreting-performance-test-results/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/interpreting-performance-test-results/</guid>
      <description><p>Once a performance tests and run, it&rsquo;s disco analysis is performed and test results persisted. Results or downloadable and persisted in the <a href="https://smp-spec.io/">Cloud Native Performance</a> format.</p>
<h2 id="graphical-view">
	Graphical View
</h2>
<img src="/v0.9/guides/performance-management/images/performance-dashboard.png" />
<img src="/v0.9/guides/performance-management/images/chart.png" />
<h2 id="tests">
	Tests
</h2>
<p>For the best experience, you should compare between two or more tests of similar configuration. Tests that are configured with a high degree of variance (e.g., one test ran for a duration of 5 minutes, while another test ran for a duration of 1 hour) will produce comparisons that are more difficult to extrapolate insights from.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Managing Performance</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/managing-performance/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/managing-performance/</guid>
      <description><p>Key to the efficient operation of any infrastructure is the measurement and management of it&rsquo;s performance.</p>
<h2 id="performance-profiles">
	Performance Profiles
</h2>
<p>Performance Profile is a new and improved way to save performance test configurations, schedule performance tests, etc. Meshery Performance Profiles offers the following features:</p>
<ol>
<li>Saving Test Configurations</li>
<li>Create schedules for running tests automatically.</li>
<li>Meshery offers UI for describing the schedules which are as powerful as CRON but without the hassle of remembering its syntax!</li>
<li>All the tests performed are under Profiles which has multiple advantages like:
<ul>
<li>Access test results ran under a certain profiles at one place.</li>
<li>If running ad-hoc tests, user can anytime come back and rename the performance profiles for re-use.</li>
</ul>
</li>
</ol>
<h2 id="load-generators">
	Load Generators
</h2>
<p>Meshery provides users with a choice about the kind of load generator they prefer to use for a given performance test. Users may set their configure based on their own preference of load generator different from that of the default load generator.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Performance Management Guides</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/</guid>
      <description><p>Guides for understanding Meshery&rsquo;s ability to characterize and analyze performance of your infrastructure and applications.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Performance Management with Meshery</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/performance-management/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/performance-management/</guid>
      <description><p>This guide walks through running performance benchmarks using Meshery. Users can either use the Meshery UI, the CLI, mesheryctl or run performance tests in their CI/CD pipelines using the Meshery GitHub Action.</p>
<h2 id="installing-meshery">
	Installing Meshery
</h2>
<p>Install and login to Meshery to start running performance benchmarks. See <a href="/v0.9/installation/">Installation</a> documentation for detailed steps on how to install Meshery.</p>
<p><em>Meshery dashboard</em></p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/guides/performance-management/images/smi-dashboard.png"><img alt="Meshery Dashboard" src="/v0.9/guides/performance-management/images/smi-dashboard.png" /></a></p>
<p>If you are looking to run performance benchmarks on cloud native infrastructur, you can use Meshery&rsquo;s cloud native infrastructurelifecycle management capabilities to deploy all kinds of cloud native infrastructure on Kubernets. With Meshery&rsquo;s performance benchmarking feature, you can also deploy you application off the mesh and compare the performance and determine the overhead when the app runs on the mesh.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Using Metrics in Meshery</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/meshery-metrics/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/performance-management/meshery-metrics/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="connect-and-use-metrics-in-meshery">
	Connect and use metrics in Meshery
</h2>
<p>Meshery provides performance reports, including performance test results, node resource metrics etc. so that operators may easily understand the overhead of their cloud native infrastructure control plane and data plane in context of the overhead incurred on nodes running within the cluster. In order to generate performance test reports of infrastructure and their workloads, Meshery uses Grafana and/or Prometheus as visualization and metrics systems, respectively. This guide outlines the requirements necessary for Meshery to connect to these systems. The steps may vary depending upon the infrastructure and its configuration.</p></description>
    </item>
  </channel>
</rss>

<details>
    <summary>
    <h6>Question: What is Meshery?</h6>
</summary>
<p><strong>Answer:</strong> Meshery is a self-service engineering platform that enables collaborative design and operation of cloud and cloud native infrastructure.</p>
</details>
<details>
    <summary>
    <h6>Question: Why was Meshery created?</h6>
</summary>
<p><strong>Answer:</strong> As an open source, vendor-neutral project, Meshery was created out of the necessity to enable platform engineers, site reliability engineers, and DevSecOps teams to collaborate in the management of their infrastructure and workloads. Meshery was created as an extensible platform to serve a broad set of modern application management needs.</p></description>

    <item>
      <title>Meshery Overview</title>
      <link>/v0.9/project/overview/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/project/overview/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="meshery-is-for-all-cloud-and-cloud-native-infrastructure">
	Meshery is for all cloud and cloud native infrastructure
</h2>
<p>Meshery is an <strong>extensible engineering platform</strong> for the collaborative design and operation of cloud and cloud native infrastructure and applications.</p>
<p>Kubernetes-centric. Kubernetes not required.</p>
<p>Infrastructure diversity is a reality for any enterprise. Whether you&rsquo;re running a single Kubernetes cluster or multiple Kubernetes clusters, on one cloud or multiple clouds, you&rsquo;ll find that Meshery supports your infrastructure diversity (or lack thereof).</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Meshery Playground</title>
      <link>/v0.9/installation/playground/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/installation/playground/</guid>
      <description><p><em>Try out Meshery Playground at <a href="https://playground.meshery.io/">https://playground.meshery.io/</a></em></p>
<p>Meshery Playground is a web-based, collaborative environment that lets you explore Meshery as a cloud native manager and all of the infrastructure it manages, including multiple Kubernetes clusters, CNCF projects and applications, services, and operators that run on Kubernetes. Meshery Playground provides a sandboxed environment to experiment with different infrastructure configurations and deployment options. Its multiplayer plugins allow you to collaborate in real time with your teammates on infrastructure design and operation.</p></description>
    </item>

      <title>Meshery Operator, MeshSync, Broker Troubleshooting Guide</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/meshery-operator-meshsync/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/meshery-operator-meshsync/</guid>
      <description><div class="alert alert-info" role="alert"><div class="h4 alert-heading" role="heading">What is Meshery Operator?</div>
<p><a href='/v0.9/concepts/architecture/operator'>Meshery Operator</a> controls and monitors the lifecycle of components deployed inside Meshery-managed Kubernetes clusters. Learn more about <a href='/v0.9/concepts'>Meshery&rsquo;s architecture</a>.</p>
</div>
<p>This guide offers comprehensive for troubleshooting instructions for <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/operator/">Meshery Operator</a> and its custom controllers, <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/meshsync/">MeshSync</a> and <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/broker/">Broker</a>. Follow the steps outlined in this document to ensure a smooth Meshery deployment.</p>
<p>First, understand the <a href="/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/meshery-operator-meshsync/#meshery-operator-deployment-scenarios">Meshery Operator Deployment Scenarios</a> and the <a href="/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/meshery-operator-meshsync/#understanding-the-status-of-meshery-operator-meshsync-and-meshery-broker">Status of Meshery Operator, MeshSync, and Meshery Broker</a> to identify the deployment model fitting of your environment. Then, follow the guidance under the respective scenario to troubleshoot accordingly.</p></description>
    </item>

      <title>Troubleshooting Extensions for Local Development</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/enabling-extensions-locally/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/enabling-extensions-locally/</guid>
      <description><p>If you&rsquo;ve set up your local Meshery development environment and an extension isn&rsquo;t showing up, this guide is here to help. Before you start debugging, the most important first step is to understand the <strong>type</strong> of the component you are troubleshooting.</p>
<p>Meshery has different types of extensions that integrate in different ways. This means their failure modes and troubleshooting methods are also very different.</p>
<h2 id="step-1-locate-the-extensions-repository">
	Step 1: Locate the Extension&rsquo;s Repository
</h2>
<p>Most Meshery extensions are open source and their repositories can be found in the <a href="https://github.com/orgs/meshery-extensions/repositories?type=all">meshery-extensions GitHub organization</a>. Your first step is to find the specific repository for the extension you are troubleshooting.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Troubleshooting Meshery Installations</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/installation/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/troubleshooting/installation/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="mesherys-preflight-checks">
	Meshery&rsquo;s Preflight Checks
</h2>
<p>Anytime a <code>mesheryctl system</code> command is executed, a series of preflight checks are run. An attempt will be made to connect to the Kubernetes cluster configured in the user&rsquo;s kubeconfig as their current-context .</p>
<ol>
<li>
<p>Check whether <code>mesheryctl</code> can initialize a Kubernetes client.</p>
<p>Situation: <code>mesheryctl</code> fails to query for pods in the default namespace of the user&rsquo;s current Kubernetes context.</p>
</li>
<li>
<p>Remove <code>~/.meshery</code> to reinitialize Meshery</p>
<p>Situation: Unable to start Meshery Server with <code>make run-local</code> due to error of <code>key/value size is invalid</code></p></description>
    </item>

      <title>Deploy AWS EC2 Instances with Meshery</title>
      <link>/v0.9/guides/tutorials/aws/deploy-aws-ec2-instances-with-meshery/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/guides/tutorials/aws/deploy-aws-ec2-instances-with-meshery/</guid>
      <description><h3 id="introduction">
	Introduction
</h3>
<p>Meshery is a powerful multi-cloud management platform that enables you to configure, deploy, and manage AWS resources, such as EC2 instances. In order to manage AWS resources, Meshery uses <a href="https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/containers/aws-controllers-for-kubernetes-ack/">AWS Controllers for Kubernetes (ACK)</a>. ACK facilitates the bridge between Kubernetes and AWS services, enabling Meshery to manage AWS resources and Meshery enabling you to benefit from the enhanced experience that Meshery and its extensions offer.</p>
<p>Meshery has a number of extensions, adapters, and plugins. In this tutorial, we will use the <a href="/v0.9/extensions//"></a> extension to provide an intuitive, visual experience for configuring and deploying an AWS EC2 instance. Among other aspects,  provides an alternative to command-line tools like <code>kubectl</code> by offering infrastructure as design. Once you connect your Kubernetes cluster to Meshery, you can configure, deploy, and manage AWS resources directly from the  interface, making deployments more intuitive and collaborative</p></description>
    </item>

      <description><h3 id="introduction">
	Introduction
</h3>
<p>Meshery now supports managing Azure resources declaratively through Kubernetes by integrating with Azure Service Operator (ASO). With this capability, you can visually design, deploy, and manage a variety of Azure resources—such as Storage Accounts, Key Vaults, SQL Servers, and more—directly from Meshery’s UI. In this tutorial, you’ll install the ASO operator (without CRD pattern configurations, as Meshery will handle them), create a Service Principal and a Kubernetes secret with your Azure credentials, and use Meshery to provision Azure resources seamlessly into your subscription.</p></description>

Adapters

What are Meshery Adapters?

Part of Meshery’s extensibility as a platform, Meshery Adapters are purpopse-built to address an area in need of management that is either considered optional to the platform and/or is considered an area in which additional depth of control is needed. Adapters extend Meshery’s management capabilities in any number of ways, including lifecycle, configuration, performance, governance, identity and so on. Meshery Adapters come in different form factors, and depending on their purpose, deliver different sets or capabilities. Each Adapter registers its capabilities with Meshery Server. Meshery Server, in-turn, exposes those capabilities for you to control.

Meshery Adapters for Lifecycle Management

Adapters that extend Meshery’s lifecycle management capabilities for infrastructure do so, by offering an infrastructure-specific interface to increase the depth of control that Meshery has over a particular technology. Meshery uses adapters to offer choice of load generator (for performance management) and for managing different layers of your infrastructure. Lifecycle adapters allow Meshery to interface with the different cloud native infrastructure, exposing their differentiated value to users.

Meshery has lifecycle adapters for managing the following cloud native infrastructure.

Meshery Adapters for Performance Management

v0.8.0 Roadmap: The meshery-nighthawk adapter externalizes Nighthawk as an Meshery component.

Meshery Server allows users to generate traffic load tests using Nighthawk, fortio, and wrk2. Using the meshery-nigthhawk adapter, you can schedule, control, and execute performance tests.

Run the meshery-nighthawk adapter as an externalized load generator when you:

  1. Need a smaller sized container image for Meshery. Nighthawk binaries are dynamically linked (C++) and they need other dependencies to work. This causes bloat in Meshery Server’s image which doesn’t need them.
  2. Need adaptive load control of your performance tests, controlling the variability by which the system under test receives load. Use Meshery Server to run adaptive load tests.
  3. Need distributed load testing and the ability to horizontally scale Nighthawk, using Nighthawk’s execution forwarding service and results sink.

Adapter Deployment and Registration

Like every Meshery component, Meshery Adapters use MeshKit.

Adapter FAQs

Is each Meshery adapter made equal?

No, different Meshery adapters are written to expose the unique value of each cloud native infrastructure. Consequently, they are not equally capable just as each cloud native infrastructure is not equally capable as the other. Each Adapter has a set of operations which are grouped based on predefined operation types. See the extensibility page for more details on adapter operations.

How can I create a new adapter?

Yes, see the extensibility documentation for details how to create a new Meshery Adapter. See the Meshery Adapter Template repository as boilerplate for your new adapter.

Do adapters have to be written in Golang?

No. Adapters much interface with Meshery Server via gRPC. What language is used in that adapter is the prerogative of a given adapter’s maintainers.

Can I run more than one instance of the same Meshery adapter?

Yes. The default configuration of a Meshery deployment includes one instance of each of the Meshery adapters (that have reached a stable version status). You may choose to run multiple instances of the same type of Meshery adapter; e.g. two instances of the meshery-istio adapter. To do so, modify ~/.meshery/meshery.yaml to include multiple copies of the given adapter.

See the “Multiple Adapters” guide for more information.

Broker

Broker is a custom Kubernetes controller that provides data streaming across independent components of Meshery whether those components are running inside or outside of the Kubernetes cluster.

Broker FAQs

How many Brokers can run?

It is recommended to run one broker instance for each kubernetes cluster, However the instance itself can be scaled up based on the incoming data volume in each of the cluster. The scaling is independent of the number of instances running.

What does an HA configuration look like?

We leverage on the kubernetes functionality in terms of the High-Availability behaviour. Meaning, the broker instance gets instantiated/restarted on its own when an issue occurs. In part, Meshery-Operator is also responsible for keeping the broker functional.

What stateful characteristics does the Broker have?

All the messages that are published to the broker is persisted in-memory within the broker instance until it get consumed. Persistent-volume/Disk-space is not currently being used by the Broker.

How do I know if the Broker is working? How do I troubleshoot the Broker?

To check if your Broker instance is running smoothly (it’s deployed as a Kubernetes StatefulSet), follow these quick checks:

  • Confirm that the Broker pods are running.
  • Verify your cluster supports LoadBalancer or NodePort service types.
  • Make sure the Meshery Server can reach the Broker service.

Still seeing issues? The Meshery Troubleshooting Guide covers common problems with the Broker, MeshSync, and Operator — and offers clear steps to resolve them.

Catalog

Meshery Catalog functions much like a cloud marketplace, providing a user-friendly interface for browsing, discovering, and sharing configurations and patterns for cloud native infrastructure. With Meshery Catalog, you can easily find and deploy Kubernetes-based infrastructure and tools, making it easy to streamline your cloud native development and operations processes. A Catolog is based on the Meshery’s Catalog Schema with defined attributes.

A collection of design templates

Meshery Catalog functions much like a cloud marketplace, providing a user-friendly interface for browsing, discovering, and sharing configurations and patterns for cloud native infrastructure. With Meshery Catalog, you can easily find and deploy Kubernetes-based infrastructure and tools, making it easy to streamline your cloud native development and operations processes.

It also supports a collaborative environment, where DevOps engineers can share their experiences, feedback, and best practices with others in the community. Import cloud native patterns published by others into your Meshery Server. Benefit from and build upon each pattern by incorporating your own tips and tricks, then publish and share with the community at-large. This facilitates knowledge-sharing and helps to build a strong ecosystem of cloud native infrastructure experts.

To publish a design to catalog using Meshery UI

  1. In your web browser, navigate to the designs page (e.g. https://playground.meshery.io/configuration/designs).
  2. Find your design, and click Edit to update your design’s details.
  3. Verify that your design has the appropriate technologies, description, and any cavaets or other considerations of its purpose of use listed.
  4. Click “Publish to Catalog”, and your design is queued for review and approval by Workspace administrators.

To c

reate design pattern using Meshery CLI
  1. Ensure that you have Meshery CLI installed on your machine and it is configured to connect to your desired Meshery instance.
  2. Open a terminal or command prompt.
  3. Use the Meshery CLI commands to interact with the catalog. mesheryctl design
  4. Follow the prompts or instructions provided by the Meshery CLI help.
    • Apply design file: mesheryctl design apply --file [path to design file | URL of the file]
    • Delete design file: mesheryctl design delete --file [path to design file]
    • View design file: mesheryctl design view [design name | ID]
    • List all designs: mesheryctl design list
  5. Importing a design. mesheryctl design import -f [file-path] -s [manifest | compose | helm]
  6. Applying WASM Filter. mesheryctl filter import [file | URL] --wasm-config [filepath|string]

Publishing a Design to Meshery Catalog

  1. Request to Publish: The author submits a request to publish their design to the Meshery Catalog, including a description and any relevant considerations.
  2. Review by Admin: The workspace owner or admin reviews the design. They have the option to approve, deny, or request changes by commenting on the design.
  3. Approval Process:
    • If the admin or workspace admin approves the design, a validation is performed to ensure the design data is accurate. Once validated, the design is published to the catalog.
    • If the admin denies the design, feedback is provided for necessary changes. After the changes are made, the design is automatically published with appropriate versioning.
  4. Ongoing Management:
    • The author or workspace owner retains permission to edit, delete, or unpublish their designs from the catalog at any time.
  5. Notification for Changes: If the design no longer adds value to the Meshery Catalog, a prior notification is sent to the author, and the design may be unpublished.
  6. GitHub Workflow Integration: Once approved, a GitHub workflow is triggered to publish the design to the Meshery.io Catalog.

FAQ

Question: Why are images invisible for some designs in the Meshery Catalog?

Answer: In certain instances, the images of published designs in Meshery Catalog may not be visible due to bandwidth issues. This can occur when there are network constraints affecting the retrieval of image data. However, rest assured that the design information and other relevant details are still accessible.

Help with Meshery Catalog

If you have any questions or need assistance, reach out on the discussion forum.

Architecture

Components, their Purpose, and Languages

Meshery and its components are written using the following languages and technologies.

Components Languages and Technologies
Meshery Server Golang, gRPC, GraphQL, SMP
Meshery Database Golang, SQLlite
Meshery UI ReactJS, NextJS, BillboardJS
Meshery Provider UI ReactJS, NextJS
Meshery Operator Golang
MeshSync Golang
Broker Golang, NATS
Meshery CLI Golang
— Extensions —
Meshery Adapters Golang, gRPC, CloudEvents
Meshery Remote Providers any - must adhere to Meshery Extension Points
Envoy WAS

M Filters Rust and C++

Deployments

Meshery deploys as a set of containers. Meshery’s containers can be deployed to either Docker or Kubernetes. Meshery components connect to one another via gRPC requests. Meshery Server stores the location of the other components and connects with those components as needed. Typically, a connection from Meshery Server to Meshery Adapters is initiated from a client request (usually either mesheryctl or Meshery UI) to gather information from the Adapter or invoke an Adapter’s operation.

Adapters

In Meshery v0.6.0, Adapters will register with Meshery Server over HTTP POST. If Meshery Server is not available, Meshery Adapters will backoff and retry to connect to Meshery Server perpetually.

Figure: Meshery deploys inside or outside of a Kubernetes cluster

Adapters and Capabilities Registry

Each Meshery Adapter delivers its own unique specific functionality. As such, at time of deployment, the Meshery Adapter will register its cloud native infrastructure-specific capabilities (its operations) with Meshery Server’s capability registry.

Figure: Meshery Adapter Operation Registration

Clients

Meshery’s REST API may be consumed by any number of clients. Clients need to present valid JWT token.

Figure: Clients use Meshery’s REST API, GraphQL API, or a combination of both.

Providers

As a point of extensibility, Meshery supports two types of providers: Local and Remote.

Object Model

This diagram outlines logical constructs within Meshery and their relationships.

Meshery Operator and MeshSync

Meshery Operator is the multi-cluster Kubernetes operator that manages MeshSync and Meshery Broker.

See the Operator section for more information on the function of an operator and MeshSync section for more information on the function of meshsync.

Database

Meshery Server’s database is responsible for collecting and centralizing the state of all elements under management, including infrastructure, application, and Meshery’s own components. Meshery’s database, while persisted to file, is treated as a cache.

See the Database section for more information on the function of the database.

Meshery Docker Extension

Meshery’s Docker extension provides a simple and flexible way to design and operate cloud native infrastructure on top of Kubernetes using Docker containers. The architecture of this extension is designed to be modular and extensible, with each component serving a specific purpose within the overall deployment process.

Meshery CLI

The Command Line Interface ( also known as mesheryctl ) that is used to manage Meshery. Use mesheryctl to both manage the lifecycle of Meshery itself and to access and invoke any of Meshery’s application and cloud native management functions.

Statefulness in Meshery components

Some components within Meshery’s architecture are concerned with persisting data while others are only concerned with a long-lived configuration, while others have no state at all.

Components Persistence Description
mesheryctl stateless command line interface that has a configuration file
Meshery Adapters stateless interface with cloud native infrastructure on a transactional basis
Meshery Server caches state application cache is stored in $HOME/.meshery/ folder
Meshery Providers stateful location of persistent user preferences, environment, tests and so on
Meshery Operator stateless operator of Meshery custom controllers, notably MeshSync
MeshSync stateless Kubernetes custom controller, continuously running discovery

Network Ports

Meshery uses the following list of network ports to interface with its various components:

Component Port Purpose
Meshery Server 9081/tcp UI, REST, and GraphQL APIs
Meshery Server 80/tcp WebSocket
Meshery Broker 4222/tcp Client communication with Meshery Server
Meshery Broker 8222/tcp HTTP management port for monitoring Meshery Broker. Available as of Meshery v0.5.0
Meshery Broker 6222/tcp Routing port for Broker clustering. Unused as of Meshery v0.6.0-rc-2
Meshery Broker 7422/tcp Incoming/outgoing leaf node connections. Unused as of Meshery v0.6.0-rc-2
Meshery Broker 7522/tcp Gateway to gateway communication. Unused as of Meshery v0.6.0-rc-2
Meshery Broker 7777/tcp Used for Prometheus NATS Exporter. Unused as of Meshery v0.6.0-rc-2

Architectural Concepts

  • Adapters - Adapters extend Meshery's management capabilities in any number of ways, including lifecycle, configuration, performance, governance, identity...
  • Broker - Meshery broker component facilitates data streaming between kubernetes cluster components and outside world.
  • Catalog - Browsing and using cloud native patterns
  • Database - Meshery offers support for internal caching with the help of file databases. This has been implemented with several libraries that supports different kinds of data formats.
  • MeshSync - MeshSync ensures Meshery Server is continuously in-sync with the state of infrastructure under management.
  • Operator - Meshery Operator controls and manages the lifecycle of components deployed inside a kubernetes cluster

      <title>Adapters</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/adapters/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/adapters/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="what-are-meshery-adapters">
	What are Meshery Adapters?
</h2>
<p>Part of Meshery&rsquo;s extensibility as a platform, Meshery Adapters are purpopse-built to address an area in need of management that is either considered optional to the platform and/or is considered an area in which additional depth of control is needed. Adapters extend Meshery&rsquo;s management capabilities in any number of ways, including lifecycle, configuration, performance, governance, identity and so on. Meshery Adapters come in different form factors, and depending on their purpose, deliver different sets or capabilities. Each Adapter registers its capabilities with Meshery Server. Meshery Server, in-turn, exposes those capabilities for you to control.</p></description>
    </item>
    <item>
      <title>Broker</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/broker/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/broker/</guid>
      <description><p>Broker is a custom Kubernetes controller that provides data streaming across independent components of Meshery whether those components are running inside or outside of the Kubernetes cluster.</p>
<p><a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/broker/images/meshery-log-viewer.svg"><img class="content-image" src="./images/meshery-log-viewer.svg" alt="Meshery Log Viewer"  /></a></p>
<h3 id="broker-faqs">
	Broker FAQs
</h3>
<h4 id="how-many-brokers-can-run">
	How many Brokers can run?
</h4>
<p>It is recommended to run one broker instance for each kubernetes cluster, However the instance itself can be scaled up based on the incoming data volume in each of the cluster. The scaling is independent of the number of instances running.</p></description>
    </item>

      <description><p><a href="https://meshery.io/catalog">Meshery Catalog</a> functions much like a cloud marketplace, providing a user-friendly interface for browsing, discovering, and sharing configurations and patterns for cloud native infrastructure. A Catolog is based on the Meshery&rsquo;s <a href="https://github.com/meshery/schemas/blob/98560345814e4be036d9f0020759faf3202ec2e4/schemas/constructs/v1alpha1/catalog_data.json">Catalog Schema</a> with defined attributes.</p>
<h2 id="a-collection-of-design-templates">

</h2>
<p>Meshery Catalog functions much like a cloud marketplace, providing a user-friendly interface for browsing, discovering, and sharing configurations and patterns for cloud native infrastructure. With Meshery Catalog, you can easily find and deploy Kubernetes-based infrastructure and tools, making it easy to streamline your cloud native development and operations processes.</p></description>

      <title>Database</title>
      <link>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/database/</link>
      <pubDate>Mon, 01 Jan 0001 00:00:00 +0000</pubDate>
      <guid>/v0.9/concepts/architecture/database/</guid>
      <description><h2 id="what-are-the-meshery-databases">
	What are the Meshery Databases?
</h2>
<p>Meshery Databases function as repositories for <a href="/v0.9/concepts/architecture/meshsync/">MeshSync</a>, user preferences and system settings. Both databases are considered ephemeral and should be treated as caches. Data retention is tethered to the lifetime of their Meshery Server instance. <a href="/v0.9/extensibility/providers/">Remote Providers</a> may offer long-term data persistence. Meshery&rsquo;s APIs offer mechanisms for clients, like <a href="/v0.9/reference/mesheryctl/"><code>mesheryctl</code></a> and Meshery UI to retrieve data.</p>
<p>See the figure below for additional details of the data formats supported and type of data stored.</p></description>
